4776.dloc: Lautlehre, 'Accent und Quantität', §§28-33, pp. 43-47; the quoted §§29-31 are on pp. 44-45
4776.heavy: 'lang' = a syllable with a long vowel, as marked in Patkanov's and Castrén's transcriptions (§33: syllable quantity 'kann nicht durch allgemeine Regeln angegeben werden' and is often hard to determine); the verbal suffixes -χamd, -χumd, -χind, -χend, -kend, -as, -id, -umd, -ant, -ad count as long, -es, -eŋed, -em, -ed as short (§29); a closed final syllable with a short vowel counts as short (§30: consonant-final nouns 'wenn dieselbe kurz ist').
4776.dflt: antepenult in words of three or more syllables (§31: 'nur in mehrsilbigen Wörtern, deren zwei letzten Silben kurz sind', e.g. tévedem, tabetmet, veresem); penult in disyllables (§29a p. 44: 'Selbstverständlich ist der Accent energischer, wenn die vorletzte Silbe lang und die letzte kurz ist, als wenn beide kurz sind'); in all-short words the stressed syllable is 'kaum vor den anderen hervorgehoben' (§28)
4776.prule: Word stress lies within a three-syllable window at the right edge and is decided by vowel length: penult by default (the majority of base forms); final in disyllables whose final syllable is long and first syllable short (and optionally in consonant-final nouns, loanwords and adverbs even with a short final); antepenult only in words of three or more syllables whose last two syllables are short; in polysyllables the penult is stressed only if it is long (a listed set of long verbal suffixes counts as long).
4776.srule: Not mentioned in Patkanov & Fuchs 1906, 'Accent und Quantität' §§ 28-33, pp. 43-47 (read in full): no word-internal secondary or rhythmic stress is described; the only weaker accents mentioned are on whole words in phrases (postpositions 'immer schwach betont') and enclitics without 'selbständigen Accent'.

4777.dq: For the pronunciation of words a general rule can be made that the accent falls on the penultimate, as in Malay, Dayak, Javanese, Sundanese, &c. [Beech p. 19] ... Suffixes may cause a shift of accent to the new penult, the suffix being felt as part of the word to which it has been added [Fokker p. 109]
4777.dloc: Beech, 'Alphabet and pronunciation', p. 19; Fokker, Appendix § 8, p. 109
4777.heavy: The only condition stated is vowel quality: a penult that 'does not contain ĕ (medio-palatal, French e muet)' takes the accent; a penult containing ĕ (schwa) does not, the accent then falling on the final syllable by the examples (tĕráŋ, kĕpá', gĕnáp). No vowel-length or coda condition is stated; kasábay, bálay, dinándu (closed finals, penult accent) show that a closed final does not attract the accent.
4777.dflt: final syllable when the penult contains ĕ (given by example only, all disyllables, and all three accented examples are Bolongan forms; the sole Tarakan example mĕñjul carries no accent mark; the case of ĕ in both penult and final is not addressed)
4777.prule: Accent on the penultimate syllable of the word, provided the penult does not contain ĕ (schwa, 'medio-palatal, French e muet'); when the penult has ĕ the accent lies on the final syllable (shown by example only: Bolongan tĕráŋ, kĕpá', gĕnáp; the one Tarakan example mĕñjul is printed without an accent mark). Schwa penults are 'extremely rare' in Tarakan (= Southern Tidung proper), so the language is penult-accented in practice. Suffixes on vowel-final stems count as part of the word and shift the accent to the new penult (nusáï, naŋkúbi, sāmá-mu); the enclitic particles nia (Tar.) / na (Bol.) 'already' are not suffixes and leave the original accent in place (pupus-nia). The p. 58 footnote (pa-báïs 'to adjust', 'the accent falls on the second syllable') is consistent with the penult rule (pa-bá-ïs), not an exception.
4777.srule: Not mentioned in Beech 1908 (Fokker's Appendix § 7-8 'Accent', pp. 109-110, and Beech 'Alphabet and pronunciation' p. 19, read in full): a single word accent is described and its shift under suffixation; no secondary or rhythmic accent is discussed.

4779.dq: First, accent placement is lexically specified and the relevant domain is the word rather than the syllable. Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents.
4779.dloc: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe', pp. 15-16; sec. 4.2.1, p. 24; sec. 4.2.3, pp. 25-26; sec. 5.4, p. 53.
4779.prule: One obligatory, culminative accent per phonological word (exponents: high F0, duration, amplitude; unaccented vowels gradiently devoiced or deleted). Its position is lexically specified: simplex disyllables are either trochees /*Ø-Ø/ (high-initial) or iambs /Ø-*Ø/ (high-final, the most common disyllabic pattern), plus a third class /*L-Ø/ where a privative /L/ tone on the accented syllable is realised as a rise. No positional or weight-based rule; frequency count shows trochees and iambs 'equally distributed' with a slight iambic tendency.
4779.srule: None: accent is 'culminative (“at most one per word”)' at the level of the phonological word; no secondary or rhythmic stresses described (Sims 2017, secs. 3.7, 4-5 read; six-syllable prosodic words carry one accent mark, p. 15). Two-accent compounds are analysed as two phonological words (p. 39 fn. 20).
4779.quote: In Yonghe, accent is obligatory, culminative, and lexically specified. [...] I use the term 'accent' as opposed to 'stress' for three different reasons. First, accent placement is lexically specified and the relevant domain is the word rather than the syllable. Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents. Third, 'stress' generally refers to relative prominence, however, as will be discussed below, Yonghe accent is not strictly an issue of relative prominence…
4779.loc: Sec. 3.7 'Accent in Yonghe', pp. 15-16; sec. 4.2.1, p. 24; sec. 4.2.3, pp. 25-26; sec. 5.4, p. 53.

4779.tone: Sims 2017 analyses Yonghe as having stress-accent plus a privative /L/ tone contrast (p. 52: 'Yonghe is unique among Rma/Qiang varieties in possessing contrastive tone in addition to stress-accent'); accented toneless syllables are high, accented /L/ syllables rising, unaccented syllables low. Sims 2021 (PhD, ch. 3, p. 137) reframes the same data as 'Like most Tibeto-Burman languages, Yonghe Qiang is tonal' and describes pitch patterns: high-initial 'The accent pattern for these forms is trochaic' (p. 148); high-final 'it is difficult to say which syllable is more prominent. The first syllable is much longer than the second syllable, yet it has a lower pitch and intensity' (p. 151); rising-final (morphologically complex only) 'The accent pattern for these forms is iambic' (p. 156). Sims 2021 p. 18 says the 2017 thesis 'has issues with respect to the analysis of the tonal and accentual system'. Sims 2016 (L&L 17(3), pp. 353, 357) predates both: 'Suprasegmentals in Yonghe are not yet well understood'; 'It is not clear whether or not Yonghe has lexical tones... syllable pitch... is predictable from the stress patterns of polysyllabic words'. So the accent-vs-tone framing is unsettled between the author's own works, but no source gives a positional stress rule; the lexical accent is the constant across them.
4779.sec_quote: [p. 1, (1b)] culminative (“at most one per word”) [p. 16] Second, while accent is culminative at the level of the phonological word, some compounds consist of two (or multiple) phonological words and thus may contain two (or more) accents. [p. 39 fn. 20] Thus, these syntactic compounds may be considered to make up two separate phonological words, as they violate culminativity of accent.

4780.tone: Sharma 1979 describes a three-term lexical tone system assigned per word (Tone 1 falling-rising /\/, Tone 2 level-rising /-/ unmarked, Tone 3 rising-falling /'/; pp. 104-106), with the falling-tone syllable longer than the others (p. 105), plus utterance-level intonational pitch levels (low/mid/high) and terminal contours (pp. 107-109). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the 28 scanned pages (a full-text search over the scan: no hits for stress/accent/prominen/loud/intensity); 'emphasis' appears once (p. 105) only as an environmental feature held constant when establishing tonal contrasts. Other saved sources agree the word-level contrast is tonal: LSI Himachal Pradesh 2023 Bhotia chapter (three tones + nasalization), Hein 2017 (register tone in Tabo), Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 (two-way high/low pitch tone for the W section incl. Spiti; 'The distinction of stress is attested mainly in Balti', p. 241), Mehta 2021 (three tones per Sharma; five tone-bearing words in her Pin-valley data).

Batibo 1991 (tone paper: nominals toneless 25% / shifted H 44% / fixed H 34%; two-directional LH melody spread) mentions stress only for loanwords: p.21 'The stress in this case was interpreted as a high tone in penultimate or final syllable'; p.23 'the H (representing stress in the language of origin) has surfaced on a short, usually penultimate vowel.' 4788.tone: Two-tone system (H / L) on every syllable, including minor syllables. Monosyllables carry lexical H or L; grammaticalised morphemes may lose lexical tone and take the polar-opposite tone of the morpheme to the left; functional morphemes may be lexically toneless and get a surface tone the same way; in an iambic foot the single lexical tone aligns with the major syllable and the minor syllable takes the polar-opposite tone (OCP, LL avoided); dual formation appears to flip the verb's tone sequence (abstract p. 97; secs. 7, 9.1-9.3). 'Stress' occurs only as the adjective 'unstressed' for minor syllables (p. 99) and in the phrase-level remark 'Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus' (p. 117), which is about emphasis/focus, not word stress. Data are from one elderly speaker of the Myebon dialect; the author warns (p. 98) that tones and vowels differ significantly between Sumtu dialects and that segmental phonology is outside the paper's scope.

4789.heavy: A [+tense] vowel in the second syllable attracts main stress when the first syllable has a [-tense] vowel. Per the p. 10 feature table [tense] is + for å o u i̮ a e i and − for the short/lax ă ŏ ä̆ ö̆ ŭ and reduced ə; note 1 p. 10: 'A feszes magánhangzók időtartamukat tekintve hosszabbak a lazáknál. A legrövidebb a redukált ə magánhangzó.' (tense vowels are longer than lax ones; reduced ə is the shortest). So heavy = full (tense, longer) vowel; light = lax/short or reduced vowel. Codas play no stated role.
4789.dflt: first syllable (also when both σ1 and σ2 are full-vowelled)
4789.prule: Main word stress falls by default on the first syllable; when the first syllable has a [-tense] (lax/short, including reduced ə) vowel and the second syllable a [+tense] (full, longer) vowel, main stress shifts to the second syllable (səran 'Komi', səɣʌam 'my burbots', ḳŏrnat 'with a picture'). The 2017 edition gives only 'main stress mostly on the first syllable' and does not repeat the shift.
4789.srule: In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress falls on the third syllable (Csepregi 1998/2011 p. 14: ḳåtɣəʌamən, main σ1 + secondary σ3); the author's 2017 Russian edition generalises this to every odd-numbered syllable following the initial main stress (p. 58), i.e. binary alternation rightward from the main stress. Placement when the main stress has shifted to the second syllable is not stated.

4792.prule: STATED by Lopes 2014 p. 89: stress ('intensidade', 'tonicidade') is inherent to stems ('intensidade inerente aos temas'); compounds and stressed suffixes ('sufixos tônicos') carry their own stress without disturbing the stem's; pairs such as píra 'pele' / pirá 'peixe' differ by stress alone; no tone, no length. The primary (Barbosa 1993 p. 54, unobtained) is reported independently by Lopes 2014 p. 58 ('um valor fonológico') and Borges 2006 p. 104 ('acento distintivo') as treating stress as phonological/distinctive. NOT STATED in any reachable source and INFERRED from Lopes's ~1070 stress-marked phonemic forms: stress falls on the final syllable of the root/stem; the argumentative-case suffix -a (Lopes's own analysis, sec. 6.1.1.2.1) and a few suffixes/enclitics (-mu, -ramu, -we, -mɔm) lie outside the stress domain; under Lopes's morphology píra 'pele' is piɾ + -a ARG and pirá 'peixe' (dictionary /ipi'ɾa/) is root-final, so the one contrast offered is morphological, not lexical. Verdict set by morphology (position set by morphological structure: stem vs. tonic/atonic suffix) rests on the stated stem-inherent/tonic-suffix characterisation plus this inference; lexical (contrastive stress, the primary's own framing as carried) is the standing alternative; confidence moderate.

4793.tone: Suruí is tonal: 'A língua Suruí é tonal' (p. 24); two underlying tones /+ALT/ (H) and /-ALT/ (L), four surface pitch levels (extra-high, high, mid, low) produced by stress acting on tone (p. 24, rules RT1-RT6 pp. 25-26). Stress is a separate word property that usually but not always sits on an H syllable (p. 26). Corroboration, Bontkes, Carolyn (1988) A prosódia silábica suruí, Série Lingüística 9(2): 117-145, §1.3.4 'Acentuação', print pp. 123-124 (the section heading and its first sentences stand on p. 123; the two quoted sentences below stand on p. 124; 2007 online ed. p. 7): 'Geralmente, pode-se dizer que o acento cai num dos tons altos de uma palavra. Nas raízes verbais dissílabas, encontramos padrões tonais alto-baixo e baixo-alto, com acento na sílaba alta; enquanto nas raízes de tom baixo-baixo, o acento pode cair na primeira ou segunda sílaba.'... 'estes prefixos tendem a soar como acentuados quando ocorrem em palavras isoladas. A acentuação não tem função léxica na língua surui, mas parece influir nos padrões tonais, como se vê no caso dos substantivos possuídos.'. Bontkes thus denies a lexical (contrastive) function for stress but gives no positional rule either.

tn.quote: 1) A língua Suruí é tonal. Há poucas palavras que se distinguem entre si somente pelo tom, mas mesmo assim existe a necessidade de se considerar o tom como uma característica importante desta língua. Na superfície percebemos quatro tons que, na estrutura profunda, se reduzem a dois. Fonéticamente temos tom extra-alto [V̋], alto [V́], médio [V̄] e baixo [V̀] com os traços, [4ALT], [3ALT], [2ALT] e [1ALT], respectivamente; podemos mostrar que estes tons resultam da ação da acentuação sobre dois tons distintivos /V́/ [+ALT] e /V̀/ [-ALT].
tn.translation: 1) The Suruí language is tonal. There are few words distinguished from one another by tone alone, but even so tone must be considered an important characteristic of this language. On the surface we perceive four tones which, in deep structure, reduce to two. Phonetically we have extra-high, high, mid and low tone with the features [4ALT], [3ALT], [2ALT] and [1ALT] respectively; we can show that these tones result from the action of stress on two distinctive tones /V́/ [+ALT] and /V̀/ [-ALT].

4794.dloc: Douglin 1887, Introduction (intended for the teacher), section 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7.
4794.prule: Douglin 1887 (pre-tonal reading primer): the accent is 'usually' on the first syllable of disyllables and on the antepenult, i.e. the first syllable, of simple trisyllables; in compound words 'the accent retains the place it has in the simple words' (Douglin does not say whether a compound then carries one accent or several). Every modern description reached (Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013; Sangster & Faber 1968) describes Susu as a tone language (H, HL, LH melodies on mono- and disyllabic nouns, mora as TBU; five tone types per vowel in the pedagogical course) and states no stress or accent rule.
4794.srule: Not mentioned in Douglin 1887, Introduction 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7 (the section gives only the disyllable and simple-trisyllable accent and a sentence on compounds). Houis 1963 (ch. II section 35 fn. 1, p. 29) denies word accent altogether: 'le susu est une langue qui ne connaît que les tons et non l'accent'.
4794.quote: In words of two syllables the accent is usually placed on the first syllable: as "male" ("rice") = "má-le"; "bende" ("dirt") = "bén-de"; "kubbe" ("ashes" or "dust") = "kúb-be"; "heri" ("peace") = "hé-ri." In words of three syllables, if they are simple words, the accent is on the antepenult: as "hárrige" ("lot" or "portion"); "yámmine" ("a kingdom"); "béllaχe" ("a hand"); "wéllaχe" ("a wooden slate"). In compound words the accent retains the place it has in the simple words.

4794.tone: Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013, section 1 para. 4: "Previous work on Susu (e.g. Grégoire 1978; Houis 1963; Touré 1994, 2004) converges on the fact that mono- and disyllabic nouns, generally speaking, have one of three distinct tonal melodies, namely H, HL, and LH." Examples (1): /HH/ [túlí] 'ear', /HL/ [kérì] 'hoe', /LH/ [ɡìnɛ̀] 'woman'; TBU = mora. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur in this paper only in a bibliography title (Bamba 1991), in the tone-marking convention (acute = H, grave = L) and in footnote 10 on foot-head prominence in Bambara; nothing is said about stress or accent in Susu. Sangster & Faber 1968, 'Tones' (scan): "Just as different sounds are used to keep words apart, so are different tones used..."; five tones per vowel (neutral/mid, high, low, high-falling, low-rising) with sentence intonation superimposed; no word-stress statement (the French 'l'accentuation sur la dernière syllabe' concerns the tone that distinguishes agent from action nominals). Douglin's 1887 'accent' predates any tonal analysis: his "má-le" 'rice' puts the accent on the syllable that is L in the modern /LH/ analysis (Green et al. cite /mààlé/-type LH nouns), so it is not a rendering of H tone.

tn.quote: Previous work on Susu (e.g. Grégoire 1978; Houis 1963; Touré 1994, 2004) converges on the fact that mono- and disyllabic nouns, generally speaking, have one of three distinct tonal melodies, namely H, HL, and LH. … (1) Underlying and surface tonal melodies a. /HH/ → [túlí] ‘ear’ b. /HL/ → [kérì] ‘hoe’ c. /LH/ → [ɡìnɛ̀] ‘woman’ … Other melodies (e.g. HLH and LHL) are possible for trisyllabic nouns and nouns with phonemic long vowels in different positions. 4797.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable by default (syllabic trochees built left to right, leftmost foot is the head). Disyllables: initial stress whatever the weights (LL 'home', 'potato'; LH 'pillow', 'love'; HL huk.na 'thin', 'hate'; HH 'brinjal', 'name of Bengali month'; p. 149). Trisyllables: antepenult (initial) unless the antepenult is light and the penult heavy (closed), in which case the penult takes primary stress (LHH 'prize', LHL 'examination'; pp. 146-147, 151-152); the final syllable never carries primary stress. Heavy = closed syllable only (VC, CVC, CVVC); vowel length is not distinctive; diphthongs are monomoraic (pp. 140, 145). Data are monomorphemic, non-compound di- and trisyllables only (native words of 4-5 syllables 'very rare', p. 139). Author's parameters (p. 148): Foot type Trochee / Direction Left-to-right / Word Dominance Head Left / Quantity-sensitive 'Yes and no (Partially quantity sensitive)' / Extrametricality Yes. Transcription caveat: the PDF drops the special IPA glyphs in the example words, so only the weight patterns, glosses and stress positions are verifiable from the text; the pointed forms (ba.ɽi 'home', ba.liʃ 'pillow', baiŋ.gɔn 'brinjal') are read from p. 149.
4797.srule: Two degrees of stress. In trisyllables with an initial primary foot, a word-final heavy (closed) syllable forms its own foot and carries secondary stress: LLH ('LL)(H) 'dawn', 'fool'; HHH ('HH)(H) 'reservation' (summary table p. 156 also lists HLH ('HL)(H)). No secondary stress on a final light syllable (('LL)L 'pink', ('HL)L 'alum', ('HH)L 'property': extrametrical) nor on the final heavy of LHH (L('HH) 'prize': 'the final heavy syllable cannot form a separate foot to avoid stress clash'). Words of four or more syllables not analysed.

4799.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root ('por lo general'); monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes of verbs and nouns are unstressed; when an aspect prefix fuses with a vowel-initial root the fused word-initial syllable takes the stress (ga-+aza-beß > gázabeß); disyllabic prefixes/affixes bear their own stress on their first syllable, so a word with polysyllabic affixes can carry two or three stresses; Spanish loans keep the Spanish stress position. Position is set by root/affix identity, not by syllable count or weight.
4799.srule: Additional stresses are morphologically placed: each disyllabic prefix/affix (xele-, gule-, xulu-, belexe-, dxele-, -técaze-) carries its own stress on its first syllable (unwritten), so a word with polysyllabic affixes has two or three stressed syllables (Dxéle-dá-lýn-técaze-beß-baß); no primary-vs-secondary ranking is given and no rhythmic/alternating stress is described; words without polysyllabic affixes have one stressed syllable.

In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone (oxutéexa ‘to cook’) and before the penult a long H syllable is level-H (oxutééxela ‘to cook for’). Rising tones always become level H, so underlying /oxu-íra/ undergoes glide forma…

4800.prule: Tone language: H vs. L/toneless with one tone per mora; falling contour only on long syllables (long H penult falls, long H before the penult is level); verb tone = lexical /H/ vs. toneless root plus tense-determined melodic H. No stress or accent rule stated.
4800.quote: Some allow contour tones only on long syllables, for example Hausa and many Bantu languages (Tachoni, Dembwa Taita) have just falling tone (F) and only on long syllables. ... In these languages, short syllables can only have level tone. Languages like Tachoni, which limit tones to one-per-mora, are “contourless” in the moraic sense, but from the syllabic perspective, they allow contours. In contrast, Miya has long vowels but no R or F, and Tachoni still has only one of the expected contours on long vowels.

4800.tone: Both Odden drafts treat Tachoni purely as a tone language: H vs. L per mora, falling tone only on long syllables (and only F, not R: 'Tachoni still has only one of the expected contours on long vowels'); long H penults fall while a long H syllable before the penult is level. Odden 2015 draft p. 22 (verbatim): 'In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone (oxutéexa ‘to cook’) and before the penult a long H syllable is level-H (oxutééxela ‘to cook for’). Rising tones always become level H, so underlying /oxu-íra/ undergoes glide formation which should yield oxwiíra, but this surfaces as [oxwííra] ‘to kill’. This gives rise to a limited derivational contrast between level H versus fall on the penult.' The word 'stress' does not occur in the 2015 Bantu Phonology draft (a full-text search count 0) and occurs in the 2020 draft only for Swahili (line 29, 'a continuum between tone (e.g. Ewe) and stress (e.g. Swahili)') and in reference titles; 'accent' only as the acute-accent notation for H and in reference titles. No statement about word stress, accent or penultimate prominence in Tachoni in any source opened (Odden 2020/2015 drafts, Odden AfricanTone earlier draft, Marlo 2013, Wanjala 2014).

tn.quote: In connected speech in Tafi, both level and contour tones occur. It has three level tones: Low (L), Mid (M) and High (H). In addition to the three levels, there are gliding tones which are phonetically realised on the peak of one syllable. There are three falling tones: High-Mid (HM), High-Low (HL) and Mid-Low (ML) and two rising tones: Low-Mid (LM) and Low-High (LH). The contour tones are marked as ML, HM etc., indicating their beginning and end points. ... Tone in Tafi functions both lexically and syntactically.
tn.cite: Bobuafor, Mercy. 2013. A Grammar of Tafi. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden (LOT Dissertation Series 327). Utrecht: LOT.
